entities.name: Al-Masjid Al-Haram
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Al-Masjid al-Haram (The Grand Mosque), surrounding the Kaaba in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, is the largest mosque in the world (current capacity 2 million simultaneous worshippers, expandable to 4 million during Hajj), the holiest site in Islam, and the direction toward which 1.8 billion Muslims worldwide turn in prayer five times daily. The mosque's current structure has been expanded over 14 centuries — from the original 7th-century CE enclosure around the Kaaba to the modern multi-level complex covering 356,000 m² — making it the most continuously expanded religious building in history.

The Kaaba — the cuboid black-draped structure at the mosque's center — is regarded in Islam as the first house of worship built by Ibrahim (Abraham) and his son Ismail, later cleansed by the Prophet Muhammad in 630 CE. The Black Stone (al-Hajar al-Aswad), embedded in the Kaaba's eastern corner, is the holiest object in Islam — pilgrims circumambulate the Kaaba seven times (tawaf) and attempt to kiss or touch the stone. The Well of Zamzam, 20 meters from the Kaaba, is the spring that miraculously appeared for Hagar and Ismail according to Islamic tradition.

The annual Hajj pilgrimage — one of Islam's Five Pillars, obligatory for every Muslim who is physically and financially able — brings 2.5 million pilgrims annually, the largest annual human gathering on Earth. Saudi Arabia has invested $100+ billion in mosque expansion since 1955, creating the current multi-level structure with 9 minarets (the tallest reaching 89 meters). The 1979 seizure of the mosque by Juhayman al-Otaybi and 500 followers — ended by a bloody military operation — was the most dramatic act of religious violence in Saudi history.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Al-Masjid al-Haram — the qibla toward which 1.8 billion Muslims pray five times daily and the destination of 2.5 million annual Hajj pilgrims — is the most continuously venerated sacred site in world history and the physical focal point of the world's second-largest religion.
